2. The relevant facts are that the present petitioners as First party filed a petition on 30.1.04 under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against the opposite parties nos.1 and 2 and 4-33 for drawing up a proceeding in respect of the disputed land measuring of 13.72 acres and to restrain members of the 2nd party from disturbing their possession. Prior to that, the 2nd  party as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit no. 30 of 94 (previous. number being Title Suit no. 20/92 Borguna, and 121/55, Barisal), in the Court of Joint District Judge, for establishment of title, confirmation of possession and also for partition; and a preliminary decree was passed in that suit giving saham of 6.80 acres to the plaintiffs —2nd parties and 11.10 acres to some of the defendants of that suit on 8.7.03. The land of the proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure also falls within the said decretal land. The First party petitioners preferred Title Appeal No. 63 of 2003 against the said decree before the District Judge, Borguna and operation of the judgment and decree was stayed on 7.8.03. Since the 2nd parties have threatened first party and tried to reap away the paddy from the disputed land by force thereby causing apprehension of breach of peace, the first party had to initiate the proceeding under sections 144/145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure during pendency of the Title Appeal no. 63 of 03. On the basis of a police report about the allegation of having apprehension of breach of peace, the Magistrate had drawn up the proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on 24.12.03 restraining both the parties from entering into the case land. He also appointed Officer-in-Charge of the Police Station, Borguna, as Receiver of the disputed land by the same order. 

 9. After filing of Title Appeal no. 63 of 2003, the appellants (first party) submitted an application for staying operation of the judgment and decree appealed against which was granted by the learned District Judge, Borguna on 7.8.2003 vide Annexure-E. Subsequently, on 13.11.03, the appellants- first party filed an application before the Magistrate, Borguna under section 144/145 Cr.P.C. for initiating a proceeding against the said decree holder 2nd party; and the Magistrate, on obtaining a police report dated 4.12.03 (Annexure-B), had passed the disputed order dated 24.12.03 drawing up a proceeding and appointed a Receiver by the same order. He also restrained both the parties from entering in the case land which includes the decretal land of the other side. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has strenuously argued that since the decree of the trial Court was stayed by the Appellate Court, the appeal, being a continuation of the original suit, was nothing but a pending suit and there having no injunction order of the Civil Court regulating possession of the parties at the relevant time, the Magistrate acted properly in accordance with provisions of section 145 Cr.P.C. But such type interpretation, if considered acceptable, will create a far reaching effect and a party, already involved in the Civil Case claiming title and possession, shall get scope to go to the criminal Court to take undue advantage against the rival party and dislodge existing possession through appointment of Receiver. Section 145 Cr.P.C. is intended only to provide a quick temporary remedy for prevention of breach of peace arising out of claim and counter claim of possessory right in the immoveable property. The object of the section 145 is to enable the Magistrate intervene and pass a temporary order regulating possession - in the disputed land until the actual right of one party is fully determined by the competent Civil Court. So in the absence of such a decision or decree of the Civil Court, the Magistrate can proceed under this section to determine disputed question of possession. But when a decision has already been arrived at by the competent Civil Court relating ownership and possession, it should be respected by the Magistrate. There should not be any scope to unsettle the matter of possession by giving appointment of a Receiver and dispossess one party to the disadvantage of another and pave the way to dispossess any party as has been done in the present case. It is true that the decree of the Civil Court .was under challenge before the Appellate Court and it is yet to be made final keeping operation of the decree stayed till disposal of the appeal, so that the decree can not be put to execution till it reaches its finality. But such stay order does not mean that any party to the suit or appeal will take advantage of the situation and avail of the forum of the Magistrate Court in order unsettle the existing decision of the Civil Court regarding possession of the parties through appointment of a Receiver. Since the Appellate Court is already in the seisin of the matter including adjudication of possessory right of the parties over it, it has got exclusive authority to decide whether the verdict of the trial Court is correct or not. Till such final decision, change of possession in the subject matter, as found by the trial Court, is not expected to be interfered with by the Magistrate under section 145 Cr.P.C. The aggrieved party is, however, be liberty to seek restraining order before the Appellate Court during pendency of the Appeal, if so necessary. Since there is pending appeal over the dispute, after having a decree of the trial Court regulating the questions of right, title and possession and there was order of status-quo during long pendency of the suit from 1.12.1992 to 8.7. 2003, we hold the view that the Magistrate having no jurisdiction had illegally entertained the proceeding under section 145 Cr.P.C. and appointed a Receiver having full knowledge about the decree of the Civil Court. The facts and circumstances of the present case, if considered properly, definitely come within the ambit of the broad principles enunciated in the reported decisions already cited above wherein it is held that when the Civil Court is already seized with the question of regulating possession of the land between the same parties, the jurisdiction of the Magistrate under section 145 Cr.P.C. is ousted.
